authority: One shared curriculum, one universal core, and five role lenses. The lenses change application, examples, coaching, and portfolio evidence. They do not duplicate or approve curriculum.

model.headline: One foundation. Five ways to apply it. One accountable pilot.
model.description: Every participant completes the same One Water AI journey, then applies it through the lens of the decisions they influence.

pathways.title: One Water AI Core
pathways.audience: Everyone who influences water, wastewater, stormwater, technology, finance, governance, public policy, products, or organizational change.
pathways.headline: Understand the whole system before you change one part of it.
pathways.promise: Build a common language for AI, data, governance, water operations, economics, human authority, and implementation so every profession can make better decisions together.
pathways.problem: AI programs fail when specialists use different language, work from disconnected evidence, or optimize one function without seeing the consequence elsewhere in the system.
objectives: Explain AI, retrieval, workflows, agents, and knowledge graphs in plain language.
Connect an AI idea to water service, evidence, affected people, decision rights, and consequence.
Choose the least complicated architecture that can perform a bounded task.
Evaluate data readiness, provenance, permissions, failure, cost, and human review.
Build and defend a governed 90-day pilot with measurable stop and success conditions.
outcomes: A shared One Water AI decision vocabulary
A data and knowledge readiness map
A defended 90-day pilot and one-year roadmap
examples: A drinking-water team distinguishes advisory support from treatment authority.
A wastewater team connects permit evidence, maintenance history, and shift decisions.
A stormwater team combines maps, inspections, rainfall, and public reports without hiding uncertainty.
pathways.analogy: Think of the core as the legend on a shared system map. Every profession sees a different part of the network, but the legend lets them interpret the same evidence together.

pathways.title: Leadership and Public Value
pathways.audience: General managers, executive directors, C-suite leaders, elected officials, board members, public administrators, and cross-functional One Water leaders.
pathways.headline: Lead the system, not the demonstration.
pathways.promise: Connect public purpose, service, evidence, risk, investment, workforce, and human authority into decisions the organization and community can understand.
pathways.problem: Leaders are asked to approve AI before the organization can explain the problem, evidence, operating consequence, full cost, or accountable owner.
objectives: Ask the questions that reveal hidden assumptions, unsupported claims, and unclear authority.
Compare opportunities by public value, readiness, consequence, affordability, and trust.
Define an operating model with named decision rights and escalation.
Explain a staged AI roadmap to technical, operational, financial, and public audiences.
examples: A board challenges an AI purchase using a public-value and consequence record.
A utility executive sequences data, workforce, security, and pilot investment instead of funding a stand-alone demo.
pathways.analogy: The leader is the conductor, not every instrumentalist. The work is to keep specialists in time, preserve their authority, and make the complete performance accountable.

pathways.title: Operations and Technical Delivery
pathways.audience: Operators, maintenance professionals, engineers, asset managers, capital-delivery teams, planners, laboratory teams, and utility technical leaders.
pathways.headline: Keep the physical system at the center of the digital decision.
pathways.promise: Use AI as bounded support for operations, maintenance, engineering, planning, and delivery while qualified people remain accountable for the system.
pathways.problem: Digital tools become unsafe or useless when they are detached from field conditions, operating procedure, asset history, professional judgment, and the official record.
objectives: Connect field observations, records, models, requirements, and decision history.
Design support workflows that preserve operator and professional authority.
Test usefulness and failure against realistic water, wastewater, and stormwater cases.
Create an evidence-backed technical pilot with review and stop conditions.
examples: An operator retrieves the approved procedure and exception history but remains the decision maker.
An engineer traces a requirement from planning through design change, field condition, cost, and approval.
pathways.analogy: A clean digital model is a drawing. Operations is the pressure test. The system is only credible when it survives contact with the field.

pathways.title: Finance, Administration, and Governance
pathways.audience: Finance executives, budget professionals, administrators, clerks, records teams, procurement, legal, privacy, risk, audit, and assurance professionals.
pathways.headline: Make every dollar, record, approval, and consequence traceable.
pathways.promise: Connect records, cost, procurement, risk, privacy, approvals, and public accountability so useful AI can move without losing control of the decision.
pathways.problem: The apparent price of AI often excludes data repair, integration, review, security, change, failure, records, and exit cost.
objectives: Trace the official record, source, approval, and retention boundary.
Build a complete cost and value baseline rather than a model-price estimate.
Evaluate vendors, permissions, privacy, risk, and segregation of duties.
Create a defensible investment, procurement, and assurance record.
examples: A clerk distinguishes a helpful draft from the official record and the authority to release it.
A finance team prices the complete operating system, including review, security, integration, change, and exit.
pathways.analogy: The governance record is the chain of custody for a decision. If the handoffs disappear, the answer has no more standing than an unlabeled sample bottle.

pathways.title: Data, Technology, and AI
pathways.audience: Chief AI Officers, CIOs, CISOs, data leaders, enterprise architects, developers, security teams, data stewards, and technical product owners.
pathways.headline: Connect the technology decision to the utility consequence.
pathways.promise: Design architecture, context, identity, tools, evaluation, security, and orchestration around the real work and authority of a One Water organization.
pathways.problem: A technically impressive system can still fail because its sources, permissions, evaluation, operating owner, cost, or stop conditions are missing.
objectives: Choose among chat, retrieval, workflow, single-agent, and multi-agent patterns.
Design trusted context with metadata, lineage, provenance, and permission.
Define identity, least privilege, evaluation, incident, and escalation controls.
Build and defend the smallest useful architecture for a real utility task.
examples: A Chief AI Officer selects retrieval instead of an agent because the task needs evidence, not autonomy.
A security lead limits a tool to approved read-only records and verifies every request and result.
pathways.analogy: Connecting a tool is like issuing a badge. The badge does not decide the job, the allowed rooms, the supervisor, or when access must stop.

pathways.title: Builders, Advisors, and Solution Partners
pathways.audience: Product builders, entrepreneurs, vendors, consultants, advisors, integrators, researchers, and people who want to create something useful for the water sector.
pathways.headline: Build the thing, then prove it belongs in the real system.
pathways.promise: Move from idea to a useful, testable, procurement-ready pilot without skipping the user, operating context, evidence, security, economics, or authority.
pathways.problem: Water-sector ideas often begin with technology and reach the user, evidence burden, integration boundary, procurement path, and operating consequence too late.
objectives: Frame a measurable professional problem before choosing technology.
Build the smallest useful prototype and expose its failure modes.
Translate evidence, architecture, governance, cost, and adoption for a utility buyer.
Create a procurement-ready proof package and governed pilot proposal.
examples: A builder replaces a generic chatbot demo with a source-grounded workflow and visible human decision point.
A vendor presents test evidence, integration limits, full cost, and exit terms before making an outcome claim.
pathways.analogy: A prototype is a pressure test, not a showroom model. The work matters when it holds under real data, real users, real failure, and real accountability.
pathways.primaryCta: Turn your idea into a governed pilot

commonQuestions.question: Do I need to know how to program?
commonQuestions.answer: No. You need a real work context, professional judgment, and the willingness to test an idea against evidence.

commonQuestions.question: Is this one course for every role?
commonQuestions.answer: It is one shared curriculum with different application lenses. Everyone learns the same system, then applies it to the decisions and evidence of their role.

commonQuestions.question: Does the program authorize operational or professional decisions?
commonQuestions.answer: No. The program develops judgment and work products. Qualified people and organizational authorities retain responsibility for consequential decisions.

commonQuestions.question: Are outcomes, pricing, and enrollment open to the public now?
commonQuestions.answer: No. These pages are governed internal previews until claims, proof, terms, privacy, enrollment, and publication are approved.
